fatal_errors: The proposed PEMF-assisted infiltration and machine-learning optimization are not supported by any cited evidence.
The hypothesis misses the central intervention: liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.
It treats the starting material as an existing W–Cu scaffold rather than a WTaVTi dendrite–interdendrite alloy whose Ti/V-rich channels are selectively replaced by Cu.
It omits the selective Ti–Cu exchange mechanism, retention of W/Ta/V-rich ligaments, and formation of the approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.

Mechanical and irradiation durability of the finished composite are predicted without applicable evidence; the target study only screened precursor dendrites under 25 keV He+ irradiation and did not directly establish composite strength.

The cited papers concern generic HEA casting, sintering, or Mg–HEA composites and do not validate PEMF-driven Cu infiltration, W–Cu wetting, fusion irradiation resistance, or the claimed baseline advantage.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad W–Cu fabrication problem and supplies a nominally controlled comparison with microscopy, thermal, and mechanical measurements. However, it is not a reconstruction of the reported work and is not a well-supported alternative. The actual approach exploits directional chemical segregation in equiatomic WTaVTi through liquid-metal dealloying, producing aligned, bicontinuous RHEA ligaments and nearly pure Cu channels with a W-rich interface. The generated proposal instead introduces high-pressure PEMF infiltration and ML optimization without evidence that these measures improve W–Cu wetting or porosity. Its temperature range happens to include 1200 °C, but the pressure, short dwell, starting structure, and process physics disagree with the target. It also lacks quantitative thermal predictions, appropriate pure-W and precursor baselines, explicit irradiation fluence and energy limits, and the crucial distinction between proxy irradiation of precursor dendrites and testing of the completed composite. The experiment could test its own claims in principle, but irradiation conditions and statistical design are insufficiently specified, and requiring simultaneous improvement in every metric makes the falsification rule poorly resolved.
